_policy: A status of 'needs review' means the item is published on this page and does not block the build or the merge. Nothing has been inferred to fill a gap: where a value could not be confirmed from an official source it is left BLANK in the data files and recorded here.

flags.category: RESOLVED at integration — was a conflict between official sources
flags.title: Banking interval: 12 months CONFIRMED by a fourth official source; the sf.gov '24 full months' sentence is inconsistent with the Rent Board's own worked examples
flags.finding: Three official sources previously appeared to conflict: the sf.gov 'Banked rent increases' page states a skipped increase banks only if 'at least 24 full months' pass; Rent Board Rules & Regulations § 4.12(a) states 'A full 12 months must have elapsed'; and Admin. Code § 37.3(a)(2) states no interval condition at all. RESOLVED: the official page 'Increasing rents during irregular periods' publishes two worked examples that apply the 12-month interval. In the first, a lease beginning June 1, 2018 with no increase taken yields, on the June 1, 2020 anniversary, BOTH the 2.6% that became available June 1, 2019 AND the current 1.8% — the banked 2.6% having had exactly 12 months to elapse, not 24. The second example (April 1, 2016 lease, increase on the April 1, 2020 anniversary) stacks four periods on the same 12-month logic. The sf.gov banked-increases page also contradicts its own 24-month sentence in its own worked example.
flags.corroboration: The SAME SF.gov banked-rent-increases page contradicts its own 24-month sentence in its worked example: a tenancy beginning 8/1/2022 with increases skipped on 8/1/2023 (3.6%) and 8/1/2024 (1.7%) is shown as banking BOTH for an 8/1/2025 increase — the 1.7% having had only 12 months, not 24, to elapse. The SF.gov 'Learn about rent increases' page uses the same 12-month logic in its own multi-year examples.
flags.impact: Unit 2's 13.1% and Unit 1's 3.0% both stand on the 12-month interval, which is what Rules § 4.12 states and what the Rent Board's worked examples apply. The '24 full months' sentence on the sf.gov banked-increases page is recorded as an official-source defect (still published, not silently deleted) but is no longer treated as an open question.
flags.action: No longer blocking. Still worth one confirming question to a Rent Board counselor (free, 415-252-4600) since a guidance page and a regulation disagree on their face, but the analysis no longer depends on the answer.

flags.category: Unverified fact — requires owner input
flags.title: Certificate of occupancy date not established
flags.finding: The stated facts are that the building was built in 1940 and is rent controlled. Rent Ordinance coverage turns on the certificate of occupancy being issued on or before June 13, 1979, which a 1940 building will almost certainly satisfy — but 'almost certainly' is not verification, and the property's address or Assessor's Parcel Number was not supplied (and is personal information that must not be published).
flags.impact: If the certificate of occupancy post-dates June 13, 1979 for any reason (for example a rebuild or substantial rehabilitation), the units could have eviction protection only and no rent-increase cap — which would change every conclusion on this site.
flags.action: Look up the address on the SF Property Information Map, the tool SF.gov itself directs owners to use, and record the certificate of occupancy date. Also confirm no substantial-rehabilitation exemption has been granted.

flags.category: Unverified fact — requires owner input
flags.title: Condominium status and owner occupancy unknown
flags.finding: It is not stated whether either unit is a condominium, nor whether an owner occupies either unit. Both facts change the analysis.
flags.impact: Costa-Hawkins gives a partial exemption from rent-increase limits to qualifying condominiums for tenancies commencing on or after January 1, 1996 — which would apply to Unit 2 (2019) and Unit 1 (2025). Separately, AB 1482 exempts 'a two-unit property, provided the second unit was occupied by an owner of the property for the entire period of the tenancy'.
flags.action: Confirm from the deed / subdivision map that the units are not separately alienable condominiums, and confirm owner-occupancy status. Note that even a Costa-Hawkins-exempt unit remains subject to just-cause eviction rules and the annual Rent Board fee.

flags.category: Cannot be screened without owner records
flags.title: Retaliation timing screen cannot be completed
flags.finding: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(a) bars a rent increase within 180 days of specified good-faith tenant complaints about tenantability, agency complaints, inspections or citations, or the filing of a proceeding. Section 1942.5(d) bars an increase made to retaliate for lawful tenant organising. Neither tenant's complaint, repair-request, inspection or organising history was supplied.
flags.impact: A mathematically perfect increase served inside a 180-day window is still unlawful retaliation. This is the single most likely way a correctly calculated increase fails review by a tenant lawyer.
flags.action: Before serving ANY notice, review each unit's records for the preceding 12 months: repair requests, communications about habitability, Department of Building Inspection complaints or citations, Rent Board petitions filed by the tenant, and any tenant-association activity. Document the review. If anything falls within 180 days, obtain legal advice before proceeding.

flags.category: No official source resolves this fact pattern
flags.title: Did Unit 1's 4/1/2026 rental agreement reset the anniversary date?
flags.finding: Unit 1's lease commenced 2/1/2025. Two of three original occupants departed and one occupant was added, and a continuing tenancy is recorded at 4/1/2026 with rent unchanged at $3,995. SF.gov states the first annual increase may be imposed '12 months after the date the tenant's lease began', and that the anniversary date changes when an increase is imposed. No official SF source states whether executing a NEW written rental agreement with a replacement occupant — with no increase and with an original occupant still in place — resets the anniversary date. NARROWED AT INTEGRATION: the Rent Board now supplies the controlling DEFINITION — 'Your anniversary date is either: (1) The day and month of the last time your landlord increased your rent; or (2) The day and month your lease began (this applies if your landlord has never increased your rent).' Since no increase was ever imposed on Unit 1, the anniversary date is the lease commencement date, February 1, UNLESS the April 2026 document constituted a new lease. The remaining question is therefore purely factual — what was signed on 2026-04-01 — not legal.
flags.impact: If the anniversary date is still February 1, Scenario U1-A (3.0%, effective on or after 2/1/2027) is correct. If a new tenancy began on 4/1/2026, the first increase would not be available until 4/1/2027 and would use the then-unpublished 2027-28 percentage. Scenario U1-C is published with ALL dollar values left blank for this reason — nothing was estimated.
flags.action: Review the 2026-04-01 document: a new lease commencing that date moves the anniversary to April 1; a roommate-change addendum or amendment to the existing February 1, 2025 lease does not. Confirm with a Rent Board counselor (free, 415-252-4600). Source for the controlling definition: https://www.sf.gov/information--increasing-rents-during-irregular-periods

flags.category: Assumption requiring owner records
flags.title: Unit 2's complete rent ledger was not supplied
flags.finding: The only Unit 2 fact supplied is a lease commencing 6/1/2019 at $3,150. The 11.5% and 13.1% banked totals in this analysis assume NO increase was ever imposed between 6/1/2019 and today. That assumption is drawn from the absence of any other entry; it is not verified.
flags.impact: Decisive. If any increase was imposed, both the banked total and the anniversary date change. A tenant can petition on Rent Board Form 516C for a review of the entire rent history, and the Rent Board recalculates the lawful base rent from ALL increases imposed since April 1, 1982 — including increases imposed by prior owners, since 'New owners may use banked increases from prior owners' cuts both ways.
flags.action: Produce the complete ledger: the original lease, every notice of rent increase ever served, each effective date and amount, and any prior-owner records. Recompute before noticing.

flags.category: Out of scope — no facts supplied
flags.title: Capital improvement, O&M and passthrough history not explored
flags.finding: No facts were supplied about building condition, capital improvements, utility costs, bond measures, or operating and maintenance expenses. Those are separate petition routes above the annual allowable (Admin. Code §§ 37.3(a)(3)-(6), 37.7, 37.8) and were deliberately not modelled.
flags.impact: If qualifying capital work exists, additional lawful recovery may be available. Conversely, an unremedied habitability problem is a live defence: Form 516B lets a tenant petition where they 'received a rent increase notice within the last 60 days' and repairs required by law have not been made.
flags.action: Confirm there are no open repair or habitability issues before noticing. If capital improvements exist, review the petition route separately — it requires Rent Board approval before the cost may be passed through.

flags.category: STALE CONTENT ON AN OFFICIAL PAGE
flags.title: SF.gov 'Learn about San Francisco rental laws' still cites the 2024-25 rate
flags.finding: That page states: 'the allowed rent increase percentage for 2024 to February 28, 2025 is 1.7%.' The rate for the current period (3/1/2026-2/28/2027) is 1.6%. The page has not been updated since the 1.7% period.
flags.impact: Low. The correct current rate is confirmed by three other official sources (S-01, S-02, S-06). Recorded because an owner reading only that page would use the wrong percentage.
flags.action: Always cross-check the percentage against Info Sheet 571 and the Current Rates page rather than any single guidance page.

flags.category: CONFLICT BETWEEN OFFICIAL RENT BOARD DOCUMENTS
flags.title: Rent Board Form 538 states the wrong license phase-in dates
flags.finding: The official Rent Board Form 538 (2024-25 General Obligation Bond Measure Worksheet) states the § 37.15 license requirement 'applies to increases that are effective on or after July 1, 2020 for buildings with ten or more residential units. For condominium units and buildings with less than ten residential units, the requirement applies to rent increases that are effective on or after March 1, 2021.' SF.gov's Housing Inventory page gives July 1, 2022 and March 1, 2023.
flags.impact: Low for this property — under either set of dates a 2-unit building was already within the requirement long before today, so a current license is mandatory either way. Recorded because the discrepancy shows official Rent Board forms can lag the guidance pages.
flags.action: Rely on the sf.gov Housing Inventory page (July 1, 2022 / March 1, 2023) and confirm license status directly in the Rent Board Portal.

flags.finding: On the SF.gov Current Rates page, the link labelled '575 Cap. Imp. Labor Rates' resolves to 574_Cap._Imp._Imputed_Interest_26-27_7.26.pdf — the imputed-interest document, not the labor-rates document.

flags.category: INCOMPLETE OFFICIAL TABLE
flags.title: Rent Board Fee table omits the current tax years
flags.finding: The SF.gov Current Rates page is headed 'For March 1, 2026 - February 28, 2027' but its 'Rent Board Fees that can be banked' table lists only tax years 2023-2024 (3/1/24) and 2024-2025 (3/1/25), at $29.50 tenant / $29.50 landlord. The 2025-26 and 2026-27 amounts are absent.
flags.impact: The current-year bankable Rent Board fee amount is therefore left BLANK in the data files. It is a small but real component of lawful recovery (a landlord may pass 50% of the annual fee to the tenant and may bank it), and it is not included in any figure published on this site.
flags.action: Obtain the current fee from Form 573 Rent Board Fee History on the Current Rates page, or from the Rent Board Fee page. Do not assume the $29.50 figure still applies.

flags.category: PENDING LEGISLATION — could change the answer
flags.title: Proposed cap on banked rent increases
flags.finding: Third-party news reporting dated September 17, 2026 describes San Francisco supervisors introducing legislation that would limit banked rent increases to 10% annually and require landlords to inform tenants of rent increase limits and rights. This is NOT an official source and is deliberately not linked from this site; no enactment was found in any official Rent Board source reviewed, including the Rent Board News index checked at integration on 2026-11-06, whose most recent items are dated August 7, 2026 and January 23, 2026.
flags.impact: If enacted as described, it would directly cap Unit 2's Scenario A/B total, which is currently computed at 13.1%. Unit 1's 3.0% would be unaffected.
flags.action: BEFORE serving any notice on Unit 2, check the official Rent Board News page and the Board of Supervisors' legislative tracker for any enacted amendment to Admin. Code § 37.3(a)(2). Re-run the calculation if it has changed. Treat the 13.1% figure as provisional.

flags.category: Repo review finding
flags.title: Repository as received contained no project content
flags.finding: At the start of this session the repository contained exactly one file: README.md, 17 bytes, holding the single line '# RentincreaseSF2' with no trailing newline. There was no data, no site, no .gitignore, no LICENSE, no COORDINATION.md, and one commit ('Initial commit', 3ed3b19). GitHub Pages was ALREADY ENABLED and configured for a legacy Jekyll build from the root of main — meaning the published URL was serving nothing useful before this work. No pre-existing data existed to audit line by line.
flags.impact: There were no prior findings, tables or figures to verify or contradict. Every figure on this site was sourced fresh in this session.
flags.action: A .nojekyll file has been added so GitHub Pages serves the static site without Jekyll processing. Consider adding a LICENSE.

flags.category: Analytical — owner decision required
flags.title: Unit 1 and Unit 2 lawfully receive very different increases
flags.finding: Applying the same written policy to both units produces 3.0% for Unit 1 and 13.1% for Unit 2. The gap is entirely a function of tenure length and skipped-increase history: Unit 1's tenancy began 2/1/2025 with one skipped increase, Unit 2's began 6/1/2019 with seven skipped increases.
flags.impact: This is the substance of the discrimination question. A differential is NOT unlawful merely because it is large; what matters is whether it flows from a documented, neutral, uniformly applied policy rather than from a protected characteristic. See the Anti-Discrimination page for the full analysis.
flags.action: Adopt the single written policy set out on the Anti-Discrimination page, apply it to both units, and retain the per-unit computation sheets as the evidentiary record.

flags.category: No official source exists
flags.title: No government data compares corporate and individual landlord increase behaviour
flags.finding: No official government source was found that quantifies how large corporate landlords set rent increases differently from individual owners in San Francisco. Any statement of the form 'corporations typically raise rent by X%' or 'individual owners usually do Y' would be unsourced.
flags.impact: The Corporate vs Individual Owner page answers the question STRUCTURALLY instead — using the verified statutory differences in how the law treats corporate and individual owners (Costa-Hawkins and AB 1482 entity disqualifications, the § 37.10C algorithmic-pricing ban, Housing Inventory obligations) — and expressly declines to publish any unverifiable behavioural statistic.
flags.action: None. This is a deliberate limitation, recorded so that a reader does not mistake the absence of statistics for an oversight.

flags.category: Compliance gate — cannot be verified externally
flags.title: Rent increase license status unknown
flags.finding: An annual or banked increase imposed while the owner is unlicensed is NULL AND VOID in its entirety under Rent Board Rules § 13.14, regardless of whether the percentage and the notice were correct. License status is visible only through the Rent Board Portal and depends on the owner's own Housing Inventory filings. It cannot be verified from outside.
flags.impact: This is a complete defence for a tenant and the most commonly missed requirement. A 2-unit building has been within scope since March 1, 2023, so filings for March 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 must all have been made.
flags.action: Log in at portal.sfrb.org and confirm a current rent increase license is on file for BOTH units, and that the Housing Inventory submission for the current year was made by March 1. If any year was missed, file now — late submissions are accepted with no monetary penalty, but the license must be in effect ON THE EFFECTIVE DATE of the increase, not merely before the notice is served.

flags.category: Residual privacy risk — owner decision required
flags.title: A public site plus exact rents leaves a re-identification path
flags.finding: This repository publishes to a public GitHub Pages URL. Even fully anonymized, a determined reader could combine the ZIP code (94122), the 1940 construction year, the two-unit size and the exact base rents ($3,995.00 and $3,150.00) with other public records — including the PUBLIC Rent Board Housing Inventory, which publishes owner name, business contact information and base rent in $250 increments — to attempt to identify the property.
flags.impact: The base rents are not withheld because the owner expressly required dates and amounts to be preserved unchanged, and because they are the entire basis of the analysis. Names, address, APN and every occupant identity ARE withheld and are protected by a build-time PII sweep that fails the build.
flags.action: Two mitigations exist and were deliberately NOT applied unilaterally, because both are the owner's decision: (1) make the repository private and use a private Pages deployment; (2) round the published rents to the nearest $50 while keeping exact figures in the internal working copy. Neither changes any legal conclusion.

flags.category: NEW LAW — in force since 2026-02-09
flags.title: Demolition and major-renovation tenant protections now in force
flags.finding: Legislation announced by the Rent Board on January 23, 2026 amends both the Planning Code and the Rent Ordinance and took effect February 9, 2026. It adds a new just cause for eviction at § 37.9(a)(17), narrows § 37.9(a)(10) to the permanent removal of a single unit, requires replacement of demolished units, bars demolition permits for five years after certain harassment or a non-compliant buyout, obliges the Rent Board to hold an investigative harassment hearing within 45 days, and gives a lower-income tenant displaced more than three months by a § 37.9(a)(11) capital-improvement eviction additional monthly payments for up to 39 months.
flags.impact: Not engaged by a lawful annual or banked rent increase, so it does not change any figure on this site. It is material to two open flags: F-09 (if capital-improvement work is ever contemplated, temporary displacement now carries far larger relocation exposure for lower-income tenants) and F-10 (this is now the authoritative official description of Rent Board harassment proceedings). Updated Rent Board forms were stated to follow the effective date.
flags.action: Read the linked announcement before any capital-improvement, buyout or withdrawal decision. For a rent increase specifically, no action is required. The announcement links the full legislation text on the Board of Supervisors' Legistar portal (File record reached from the announcement page); the GUID was truncated in the fetched copy, so no direct citation is published here rather than a malformed URL.
